o: Can all elements be split into groups of exactly k pairwise-distinct values? Example 2 shows duplicates may exist ([3,5,2,2] with k=2 works since the two 2's land in different groups). Necessary conditions: n divisible by k, and no value occurs more than n/k times (each occurrence needs its own group). These are also sufficient via round-robin assignment: process values in decreasing frequency, distributing occurrences across groups cyclically — since freq ≤ n/k, no group receives the same value twice.
k: Feasible ⟺ n % k == 0 and max frequency ≤ n / k.
Sufficiency follows from a greedy round-robin assignment ordered by decreasing frequency (a classic scheduling argument).
Counting with a hash map gives everything in O(n).

a.i: Count frequencies; verify divisibility and the max-frequency bound. By the round-robin exchange argument these conditions are sufficient, so no explicit construction is needed.
a.t: O(n) — one counting pass plus a scan of distinct values.

a.i: Actually build the groups: sort distinct values by frequency descending, then deal occurrences like cards into g = n/k groups cyclically. If any group would receive a repeated value (equivalently, a frequency exceeds g), report failure — this makes the sufficiency argument concrete and debuggable.
s: Count frequencies; g = n/k; fail if any freq > g.
Deal each value's occurrences to groups 0,1,…,g−1 cyclically; success if the dealing completes.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting distinct values by frequency.

w: Approach 1 is the clean interview answer; be ready to justify sufficiency with the round-robin/decreasing-frequency argument (Approach 2 makes it tangible). Pitfalls: forgetting the divisibility check, and assuming distinctness of the whole array is required (it is not — only within groups). Follow-up: reconstruct and return the groups, or handle groups of varying sizes.
